questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Tom Jones in six volumes and eighteen books
questions.learningObjective: read a book's division into parts as evidence about a planned structure
questions.stem: Fielding's The History of Tom Jones was published in 1749 in six volumes, divided into eighteen books whose titles state how much time each covers, from twelve hours to a year. What does that titling tell a reader the author thought he was doing?

options.text: That the book will be uneven, since chapters of different lengths cannot be fitted into a single plan
options.misconception: treats variable length as evidence of no plan, when the titles themselves record a plan

options.text: That the book is a chronicle, since a narrator who measures his chapters in hours and weeks has promised a reader the shape of a life rather than a sequence of scenes
That the volumes were sold separately, since a publisher issuing six volumes is not selling one book at all
options.misconception: conflates a publisher's issue with a set of independent works

options.text: That the plot is unimportant, since a writer who spends a title on elapsed time has decided the clock is the story
options.misconception: infers a claim about the plot from a titling convention

questions.explanation: The titles are the clearest statement of method the book makes. Naming each book for the quantity of time it covers tells a reader that this narrative is being measured, and a measured narrative is a chronicle-shaped thing: it proceeds, it accumulates, and it can afford digression because the clock will not run out. That is why the book can contain, in one of its few deliberately slow stretches, a long conversation on a hillside, and why the slow stretch is not an embarrassment but the consequence of the promise the titles have made. It also explains the shape a reader meets in the paper: a narrative voice that keeps stopping to speak to the reader about method, promise and pace. A book titled for its content would make a different promise, and so would a book divided without reference to time. The second option mistakes a controlled variation for an absence of design, and the last two draw large conclusions from an ordinary publishing practice.
questions.hint: Ask what a title naming hours and weeks is promising the reader.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The digressive opening chapter of each book in Tom Jones
questions.learningObjective: recognise a structural convention and the work it does
questions.stem: In Tom Jones the first chapter of nearly every book is a digression rather than an event: one opens with a sheet of paper described at length, another announces a general account of human nature, another introduces the conventions of a narrative. What is the method doing at these junctions?

options.text: Delaying the story, since a reader who must pass through a chapter of theory before every twenty chapters is being held back from the plot
options.misconception: reads a declared convention as a pacing failure

options.text: Showing off, since no narrative needs to explain itself and a chapter given to method is a chapter given to vanity
options.misconception: reduces a formal decision to self-advertisement

options.text: Announcing, at every seam, what the reader is about to be given and on what terms, so the book's form is argued as it is used
Compensating for a weak plot, since a long book with a thin story fills the gaps with talk about the story
options.misconception: infers compensation, which is a claim about the writer's motive

questions.explanation: A convention repeated at every junction becomes an argument. A narrative that pauses at the start of each book to say what it is about to do is not stalling; it is putting its terms on the table, and a reader who accepts the terms has agreed to a contract in which digression is part of the reading and not an interruption of it. That agreement is why the digressions can be enjoyable: they are the one place where the book is directly concerned with how it is being made, and a reader who enjoys the making will enjoy them. It is also why the convention is a form of honesty. Fielding's narrative voice is not a decorative persona; it is a narrator with opinions about fiction, and the first chapter of each book is where those opinions are stated before the story asks for patience. The second option treats a promise as a delay, the third treats a formal decision as an indiscretion, and the fourth imputes a motive the book does not state.
questions.hint: Ask why a book would repeat a convention at every seam rather than once.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The mock-heroic hunt passage in Tom Jones
questions.learningObjective: recognise a classical register being dropped on purpose
questions.stem: A passage in Tom Jones describes a hunt at length in the vocabulary of epic battle, comparing the hares to an army hemmed in by a cruel and cunning enemy, and then ends by announcing, in plain words, that it is now midnight. What is the joke and what is it for?

options.text: It is a slip, since a writer who has been careful for six volumes cannot suddenly be careless about register
options.misconception: supposes a sustained joke cannot be intentional

options.text: It is a summary, since the plain sentence at the end is telling the reader what has happened in words too long to read
options.misconception: treats a closing remark as a substitute for a scene rather than as a joke

options.text: It is a satire on hunting, since a passage about hares and horses must be attacking the sport rather than the style
options.misconception: confuses a parody of a register with an attack on the activity inside it

options.text: It is a deflation, and it is deliberate: the grandeur is sustained long enough for a reader to feel its scale and then taken away in a single flat sentence

questions.explanation: A mock heroic needs the disproportion to be real before it can be funny, and that is why the passage does not wink. The vocabulary of armies, sieges and a cruel cunning enemy is carried at full stretch, without a hint that the writer finds it funny, and the reader is drawn in far enough to have accepted the scale. The plain sentence then removes the whole apparatus in nine words. A parody that announced itself would be a joke about parody; this one is a joke about the habit of inflating small occasions, and it works by the delay between the two registers. What the reader is being trained in here is the same skill the digressive first chapters are training: to notice a claim being made about scale and to check it. The second option cannot account for the delay, which is the whole mechanism. The third and fourth both mistake the register for the subject, which is the error the mock heroic exists to expose.
questions.hint: Ask why the plain sentence comes at the end rather than the start.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Pamela's epistolary form and its two-year printing
questions.learningObjective: read a novel's form as a constraint on what its plot can contain
questions.stem: Richardson's Pamela appeared in 1740 and 1741 in two volumes made up entirely of letters, and a continuation followed in 1741 after the first ending was attacked as too neat. What does the form make possible and what does it make difficult?

options.text: It makes the story verifiable, since a letter is a document and a document cannot lie about the facts it records
options.misconception: supposes a document cannot lie, which is the assumption the form exploits against the reader

options.text: It makes a narrow interiority possible, since a letter is a partial and self-serving account, and it makes simultaneous action elsewhere difficult, since no letter can report it
It makes the plot impossible, since a story told in letters has no action in it and only report survives
options.misconception: denies a story told in letters the power to narrate action at all

options.text: It makes the ending a matter of taste, since a reader who dislikes the first ending can simply read the continuation and have a different book
options.misconception: treats a sequel as an alternative edition of the same work

questions.explanation: An epistolary novel is a novel made of documents written by people with interests, and both halves of that fact matter. The form is superb at interiority, because a letter can report a state of mind at the moment it exists and cannot be checked by the writer afterwards; that is where its power and its unreliability come from at once. It is correspondingly poor at simultaneous action, since a letter is necessarily late about everything it does not mention, and a plot that depends on two things happening at once has to be managed by a reader assembling the pieces. The first ending and the continuation make the constraint visible: a conclusion that felt too tidy inside a form built out of one woman's letters was going to be a conclusion about the letters, and the sequel is a different set of documents about the same matter. The second option believes documents are reliable, which is exactly the belief the form trains a reader to abandon. The third and fourth overreach in opposite directions.
questions.hint: Ask what a letter can report and what it can only guess at.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Tristram Shandy printed in instalments and never finished
questions.learningObjective: read an unfinished book's shape as a consequence of its printing
questions.stem: Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy was printed in instalments between 1759 and 1767 and never finished: the last volume breaks off in the middle of a sentence, and one volume contains a page that is simply black. What do the instalments and the black page tell a reader about the book's form?

options.text: That the black page is an error, since a page printed entirely black cannot have been intended and must be a mistake in the press
options.misconception: assumes an effect is an accident, which is the reading the book invites and defeats

options.text: That the unfinished ending proves the author had lost interest, since no writer stops mid-sentence by design
options.misconception: supplies a motive that the book's whole procedure denies

options.text: That the book's shape is an instalment, so the reader meets it in pieces and the blank and the black page are places where the book shows the reader its own surfaces
That the instalments are the real divisions, since a book printed in parts can only be read as a set of separate works
options.misconception: treats a binding choice as a change of work

questions.explanation: A book published in instalments is read in instalments, and a book that knows this uses the fact. Breaking off mid-sentence is the one gesture available that cannot be mistaken for a lost page, and printing an entirely black page makes the reader hold the object rather than the text: the surface of the book is now the subject. Both are ways of saying that a book is made of paper and sequence, and both are only funny or only powerful because a reader has spent a volume or two pretending otherwise. That is also why the volume titles announce themselves as numbers and a half. A reader who calls the black page a misprint has made the standard error; the standard error is treating a book as a transparent window when the book is also a thing. The third option supplies a biographical motive that the procedure itself denies, and the fourth confuses a binding decision with a change of work.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has to do to see a page that carries no words.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Candide and the thesis its last chapter states
questions.learningObjective: read a conclusion's argumentative form rather than its content
questions.stem: Voltaire's Candide, first published in 1759, runs to twenty-two chapters, and the last chapter abandons the travellers and argues in the narrator's own voice about how people ought to live, ending by proposing a short practical rule rather than a system. What does that shape of ending do?

options.text: It abandons the book, since a conclusion that abandons the characters for an argument has stopped being a novel
options.misconception: treats an argument in a narrator's voice as the end of the form

options.text: It retracts the book, since a writer who adds a moral after mocking other writers' morals is giving up the right to mock
options.misconception: supposes a comic argument at the end undoes a comic argument throughout

options.text: It dates the book, since a chapter that argues about how to live belongs to a different moment from the chapters that mock a philosopher
options.misconception: infers a date from a change of register

options.text: It closes the book's argument in the form the argument has been about, since a book that has mocked every system must end by making one modest claim of its own

questions.explanation: The ending is the argument, not an appendage to it. A book whose chapters are occupied with demonstrating that every available scheme of life produces absurdities is not thereby neutral; it has made a case, and a case about systems has to end somewhere. Having refused every large answer, the book can only close with a small one, and the disproportion between the size of the rule and the size of the wreckage is the last joke and also the last point. The abandonment of the travellers is part of the form rather than an exit from it, because the book has had a narrator all along who has been commenting, and a concluding chapter in that voice is a continuation of an established practice. The second option defines a novel so narrowly that most first-person novels would fail it. The third mistakes a rule for a retraction. The fourth treats a change of register as evidence of a change of date, which is a strange way to read a book.
questions.hint: Ask what a book that has mocked every system has to do at the end.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The two states of Frankenstein and their different front matter
questions.learningObjective: compare a first edition and a revised edition through their framing
questions.stem: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein was published in 1818 without the author's name on the title page, with a short address to the reader; the 1831 printing replaced that address with a longer introduction, put the author's name on the title page, and reshaped the opening so the story is no longer presented as a manuscript being edited by a fictional friend. What has changed?

options.text: The plot, since changing the opening of a novel must change what happens in it
options.misconception: assumes a change of framing changes events, which is a strong claim the evidence does not support

options.text: The contract with the reader, since a fictional editor and an anonymous title page made the reader a participant in a story's manufacture, and the 1831 text removes that participation
The authorship, since a named title page settles a question the anonymous one had left open, and everything else follows from the name
options.misconception: reduces the revision to a change of attribution

options.text: The genre, since a story about a creature is a different kind of book once the narrator is no longer inside it
options.misconception: infers a change of kind from a change of narrator

questions.explanation: What the two editions give a reader is a different position. In the first, the story reaches the reader through invented hands: a letter, a friend, a set of papers being arranged, and a title page with no name on it. That arrangement asks the reader to treat the tale as a thing being put together, which is a real effect and one a reader cannot recover once the devices are gone. The 1831 revision removes them and gives the reader a first-person narrator and a named author, which is a more familiar position and, for that reason, a loss of a specific kind. The story is not materially different and the genre has not changed; what has changed is the deal. The second and fourth options both claim more than a change of framing can do, and the third mistakes an attribution for an argument. The useful test a reader can apply is to ask what a person has to believe in order to begin, and the two editions have different answers.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has to accept in order to begin each version.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What the 1831 introduction adds about the making of the creature
questions.learningObjective: read a new preface as a claim about causation
questions.stem: The 1831 printing of Frankenstein adds a long introduction in which the writer describes a conversation about whether a dead body could be restored to life by a process of galvanism, and says that the idea of the book came to him in the middle of that conversation. What does the addition do to the book's account of itself?

options.text: It supplies a moral, since a story that begins with a conversation about electricity is a story warning against interfering with nature
options.misconception: reads a claim of origin as a moral, which is a different kind of statement

options.text: It removes the strangeness, since an explanation of how the book began makes the book's world easier to enter
options.misconception: assumes an explanation makes a story easier, which is generally the opposite

options.text: It makes the story of a scientific process the origin of the story, so that the reader now encounters a causal claim about the book before any of the book's events
It dates the book, since a conversation about a scientific process places the writer in a year when that process was being discussed
options.misconception: turns a reference to a contemporary debate into a dating instrument

questions.explanation: The addition is a claim about where a book comes from, and a claim of that kind is a real argument rather than a decoration. Placing a conversation about a scientific process in front of the narrative tells a reader that the book is about a mechanism, and it does so before the mechanism is described, which means the reader approaches the later events already holding a hypothesis. That is a considerable change of emphasis, and it makes the 1831 text more, not less, unsettling, because the question of how such a thing could be done is now asked in the book's own voice. The introduction also makes the writer's own account of the book's making a matter of public record, which the 1818 text carefully avoided. The second option converts a claim about origin into a lesson, the third assumes explanation is the same as accessibility, and the fourth treats a mention of a contemporary debate as a date, which no reference to a debate can be.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is being told before the story has begun.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Mansfield Park and the essay printed after its story
questions.learningObjective: read a work's paratext as part of the work
questions.stem: Mansfield Park, published in 1814, ends with a long essay on the novel as a form, which was also printed as a separate pamphlet in the same year, and in which the writer talks about what a novel may depict and how readers should be prepared to be disturbed. What does the essay's existence tell a reader?

options.text: That the novel is incomplete, since a book that needs a concluding essay has not managed to end its own story
options.misconception: treats a paratext as a failure of the text it follows

options.text: That the essay was written first, since a writer who begins with a theory will have had the theory in hand while composing the story
options.misconception: infers order of composition from order of print

options.text: That the two are independent, since a pamphlet and a novel are separate publications and a reader has no reason to connect them
options.misconception: denies any relation between a book and the essay issued with it

options.text: That the writer is making a claim about the kind of book she has written, and has put the claim where a reader cannot mistake it for a story

questions.explanation: An essay printed with a novel, or beside it, is an argument about it, and the essay's subject matter makes the argument unmistakable: this is a book about whether a novel may show what it has shown, and here is a writer who has thought about the question and has changed her mind in public. Printing the essay separately as well is not a sign of uncertainty; it is a sign that the claim is meant to be read by people who will not read the novel, which is a considerable thing for a novelist to do. The essay also sets up a reader contract: it warns that a novel is capable of being disturbing and asks to be judged on a wider scale than entertainment. The second option reads a paratext as a failure of the text, when the text has closed. The third infers composition order from print order, which a publisher can reverse. The fourth denies a relation that the pamphlet's existence puts beyond doubt.
questions.hint: Ask why a novelist would put an argument about novels next to a novel.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Northanger Abbey published late and dated a year later
questions.learningObjective: read a publication date as evidence about a work's history
questions.stem: Northanger Abbey was written in 1798 and 1799, kept back for nearly twenty years, and published at the end of 1817 on a title page dated 1818, after another novel. What does that sequence show about the judgement involved in publishing it?

options.text: That the writer lost interest in the novel, since a book held back for twenty years is a book abandoned
options.misconception: infers indifference from a long delay

options.text: That a writer and a publisher decided the market could not take it until the moment was right, and then dated it forward in the ordinary way
That the title-page date is false, since a book written in 1798 cannot honestly bear 1818
options.misconception: treats a forward-dated title page as a falsehood when it is a publishing convention

options.text: That the novel was rewritten for publication, since twenty years of delay will have changed the text completely
options.misconception: assumes delay entails rewriting

questions.explanation: A delay of eighteen years is not a lapse of interest; it is a decision held open. The novel parodies a fashion, and a fashion is a thing whose parody dates easily, so a writer who wanted to write it in 1798 would have been writing against a market that was not yet ready to recognise what was being parodied. What the record shows is judgement about a readership, exercised twice: once in withholding and once in releasing. The forward-dated title page is the ordinary practice of a book intended for the coming season or year, and a title-page date a year ahead of publication is not a false statement but a commercial one. The second option reads a delay as indifference, which is a very economical inference from very little. The third mistakes a convention for a lie, and the fourth assumes that twenty years of silence will have altered a text, which is not what silence does.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of judgement a writer makes by waiting and then by dating forward.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Persuasion published after its author's death
questions.learningObjective: read a posthumous publication as part of a book's history
questions.stem: Persuasion was finished in 1816 and published in the last months of 1817, after its author's death, with a title page dated 1818, and the price was raised well above what her earlier books had cost. What does that set of facts do to a reader's sense of the book's situation?

options.text: It makes the book unfinished, since an author who died before publication cannot have known where the story ended
options.misconception: infers incompletion from absence of supervision

options.text: It makes the price irrelevant, since what a book costs has never affected how it is read
options.misconception: dismisses the price as though it were not a fact about the book's reception

options.text: It makes the book a survivor, since the author could not see it published or correct it, and the price suggests the publisher expected the demand for her name to carry the book
It makes the book the last of a series, since a final publication conventionally ends a career and readers should read it as a summing up
options.misconception: turns a chronological fact into a conventional expectation

questions.explanation: Posthumous publication is a strange condition for a novel, and it produces effects that are worth naming. Nobody was in a position to correct proofs on the author's judgement, so the text a reader holds is a text that passed through other hands, and a reader who knows that will read the last pages with an ear for what has been smoothed. The price tells a different and equally useful story: a publisher charging more than usual for a book by an author whose recent work had been bought readily is making a commercial calculation about a name, and that calculation is evidence about how the book was expected to be received. Neither fact damages the novel, and together they explain a great deal about how it came to be read. The second option confuses absence of supervision with absence of completion, which are unrelated. The third throws away real evidence, and the fourth imports a convention the record does not require.
questions.hint: Ask what the price says that the date does not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Jane Eyre's three volumes and its declared form
questions.learningObjective: read a title page as a claim about a book's kind
questions.stem: Jane Eyre appeared in October 1847 in three volumes under a pen name, and its title page described it as an autobiography edited by the editor named on the page, and it was divided into thirty-eight chapters. What does that title page set up?

options.text: A legal claim of authorship, since a title page naming an editor is a statement of copyright and the book is therefore protected in the editor's name
options.misconception: reads a title page as a legal instrument, which is a different kind of document

options.text: A guarantee of realism, since a book calling itself an autobiography has promised that nothing in it is invented
options.misconception: takes the claim of autobiography as a promise of fact, which no novel can keep

options.text: A division of labour, since three volumes and thirty-eight chapters show that the book was assembled by more than one person
options.misconception: infers collaboration from a division into volumes and chapters

options.text: A reader-writer relationship, since a first-person autobiography is a claim about who is telling the story, and the named editor acknowledges that somebody made the text available

questions.explanation: The title page does a delicate piece of work. Calling a first-person novel an autobiography makes a claim about the narrator's relation to the reader, and a novel whose narrator speaks in the first person and addresses the reader directly can be said to be asking to be taken at something other than the narrator's word. The second half of the phrase, edited by, is the more interesting half: it puts a named hand between the reader and the narrator and admits that a text has been put into circulation by somebody other than the person whose voice it carries. That arrangement makes the reader a party to the book's making, which is the opposite of the fourth option's claim that a division of the material implies divided authorship. The third option is the mistake the book plays with, since a claim of autobiography is a formal claim and not a warranty. The second mistakes a title page for a document in a lawsuit.
questions.hint: Ask what the phrase about the editor admits about how the text arrived.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Jane Eyre's second edition and its dedication
questions.learningObjective: read a dedication as a professional address
questions.stem: The second edition of Jane Eyre, which appeared within a few months of the first, is dedicated to a novelist then famous for a novel of social satire. What does the dedication tell a reader about the book's standing and its author?

options.text: That the author is a man's pupil, since a dedication from a woman to a man is a recognition of a superior
options.misconception: reads a professional address as a personal one, which the form does not require

options.text: That the author is claiming a place in a professional company, and is addressing the one reader whose verdict could establish her, since the dedicatee is a practitioner of the same trade
That the first edition was a failure, since a book is only reissued with a new dedication when the first did not sell
options.misconception: infers a commercial verdict from a reissue

options.text: That the second edition is a different book, since a new dedication must be accompanied by a new text
options.misconception: assumes a change of address implies a change of text

questions.explanation: A dedication is an address, and a professional dedication does a specific job. It puts the book before a reader who is competent to judge it, who is not a relative, and whose opinion of the form is worth having, and it does so publicly, which is a claim about company rather than a request for a favour. The choice of a satirist of society is also pointed, since a novel that is going to be criticised for its plainness and its attention to material conditions is being placed beside a writer whose reputation is exactly in that line. What a reader can safely infer is a claim to standing and a chosen company; what a reader cannot infer is a relationship, a commercial verdict, or a new text. The second option turns a professional gesture into a personal hierarchy, the third invents a commercial story from a reissue, and the fourth supposes that a change of address must accompany a change of the book itself, which is not how dedications work.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of reader the author is addressing and why that reader.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Wuthering Heights and its two layers of narration
questions.learningObjective: read a nested narration as a set of claims about reliability
questions.stem: Wuthering Heights is told by a visitor who has locked himself out of a house and is being entertained by the tenant, and the tenant then recounts a long history and, inside that, quotes letters and the accounts of other people. What does this arrangement do to the reader's position?

options.text: It obscures the story, since a book that goes through three narrators cannot deliver a plot a reader can follow
options.misconception: assumes layers of narration defeat narrative order

options.text: It lends the story authority, since a book with several witnesses must be a book that was checked by more than one person
options.misconception: supposes multiple witnesses make a story more accurate, which they do not

options.text: It puts the reader at a distance from every account by one remove or more, so that the reader's task becomes the comparison of testimony rather than the acceptance of it
It makes the tenant the villain, since a man who keeps a locked-in visitor in a kitchen has something to hide and the reader is being warned
options.misconception: reads a character as a warning from the framing device

questions.explanation: Every layer of this narration is a mediation, and the reader's position is fixed outside all of them. The visitor reports what he was told; the tenant reports what he was told; and inside his account come letters and second-hand speech. Nothing reaches the reader at first hand, which means the reader cannot check anything and must instead weigh one kind of testimony against another, and a great deal of the book's effect comes from the fact that the most violent events are known to us through documents written by people with reasons to write them as they did. That is also why the framing matters: the locked-out visitor has a comic discomfort that the story inside does not, so the book establishes a norm of caution before it breaks it. The second option assumes layers defeat sequence, which is the opposite of what makes a book readable. The third mistakes many witnesses for accuracy, and the fourth reads the frame as a moral signal about the tenant.
questions.hint: Ask how many removes of telling stand between the reader and the events.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Charlotte Bronte's notice of her sister's first novel
questions.learningObjective: read a biographical notice as a claim about authorship
questions.stem: The first edition of Wuthering Heights in 1847 carried a short biographical notice, written by the author's sister, presenting the author as a reserved young woman who had published two books the public had not valued. What is that notice doing inside the volume?

options.text: Supplying the missing biography, since a novel by an unknown author needs a life attached before a reader will take it seriously
options.misconception: supposes a notice is supplying a record, when it is supplying a frame

options.text: Discrediting the earlier books, since to say the public did not value them is to say they were rightly ignored
options.misconception: reads a remark about reception as a verdict on the earlier work

options.text: Warning the reader off, since a notice that emphasises the author's shyness and isolation is a warning against expecting much
options.misconception: reads a frame that invites attention as a warning against it

options.text: Managing a reading before it starts, setting an expectation of plainness and austerity so that the book's content will be measured against a prepared scale

questions.explanation: A biographical notice inside a first volume is a piece of positioning, and its job is done before the novel opens. options.misconception: treats a subplot as padding, which is a judgement about a book's economics rather than its argument

options.misconception: reads a subplot as delay without evidence

options.text: A reliable narrator, since the third-person voice corrects the child's account by standing outside it

questions.stem: Moby-Dick opens with a chapter that extracts and glosses the word whale, and follows it with a long chapter that sorts whales into categories and sizes, and only then begins the story of a voyage. What are those two chapters doing?

options.text: Delaying the story, since two chapters of reference material before a voyage is two chapters a reader has to pay for in patience
options.misconception: reads a declared method as an unwarranted delay

options.text: Claiming authority, since a book that sorts its subject into orders is asserting that its subject can be ordered
options.misconception: infers a claim to authority from a taxonomic interest

options.text: Signalling that the book is encyclopaedic, since a text with glossaries and lists has declared itself a work of reference
options.misconception: infers a kind of book from the presence of apparatus

options.text: Saying what the book knows and how it knows it, so that a reader has been given the book's method, its sources and its categories before being given anything that happens

questions.explanation: These chapters are a table of contents written in prose. A word is taken apart and glossed, and then a subject is divided into orders and sizes, and in doing so the book tells a reader three things: what it means by its central term, where its information comes from, and that it intends to be systematic. That is a considerable gift and an unusual one, because most novels ask a reader to learn these things by inference. It also means the story that follows is being told inside a declared apparatus, and a reader who has been given the categories will notice when the story refuses to fit them, which is one of the things the story is about. The second option calls the method a delay, the third reads a taxonomic interest as a claim to power over the subject, and the fourth takes the presence of apparatus as a declaration of genre, when the apparatus is used to make a story rather than to replace one.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do after the two chapters that a reader could not do before them.

questions.topic: Moby-Dick's two titles on two sides of the Atlantic
questions.learningObjective: read a title change as a publisher's judgement about a market
questions.stem: The book published in the United States in 1851 was titled for the whale with a name attached, and the volume sold in Britain was titled simply The Whale. What does that difference tell a reader?

options.text: That the two books are different novels, since a different title must mean a different work
options.misconception: treats a title change as a change of work

options.text: That a name on a title page is a piece of information a publisher supplies, and that the two markets were being asked to buy different promises
That the author changed his mind about the whale, since a title is chosen by the writer and the writer changed it
options.misconception: supplies an authorial decision where a publisher's is documented

options.text: That the British edition is the true title, since a shorter title is the older and more honest kind
options.misconception: prefers one title on stylistic grounds, which is not evidence

The second option makes a title change into a change of work, the third credits the writer with a decision the trade made, and the fourth ranks the titles on grounds of taste, which tells a reader nothing about either book.
questions.hint: Ask who chooses a title page and what a title is for.

questions.topic: The Great Gatsby and a narrator who tells a reader how to read him
questions.learningObjective: read a narrator's self-placement as part of the book's argument
questions.stem: The narrator of The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, introduces himself early by naming the qualities he believes himself to possess and the circumstances that have kept him near other people, and he tells a reader at the outset that the account he is about to give concerns one man. What is that doing?

options.text: Apologising for the book, since a narrator who begins by saying what he is not must be unsure of his own account
options.misconception: reads a claim to standing as an apology

options.text: Narrowing the book to a case study, since a subject of one man cannot carry a claim about a country
options.misconception: turns a limited claim into an admission of inadequacy

options.text: Claiming standing and limiting the book's claim at once, since a narrator who names his own competence and then narrows the subject has told a reader exactly how much weight to put on what follows
Preparing a reader for unreliability, since a narrator who describes himself so carefully is hiding something about himself
options.misconception: infers concealment from self-description, which is a guess about the author

questions.explanation: The two sentences do different jobs and it is worth keeping them apart. The self-description is a claim to standing: the narrator is saying that he is someone whose position gives him access and whose judgement is therefore worth relying on, and he makes the claim before the evidence rather than after it, which is a mark of seriousness. The second sentence is a limit on the book's reach, and it is an odd thing to say unless the book means to exceed it. A reader who has been given both a claim and a limit is being asked to do something specific, which is to weigh one man's story carefully and then to notice how much the story is about everything else. Nothing in that suggests apology, inadequacy, or concealment. The second option treats a claim as a confession, the third mistakes a limited claim for a deficient one, and the fourth turns a narrator's self-description into a fact about the author, which a reader has no access to.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader is licensed to conclude, and what a reader is warned not to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ulysses as eighteen episodes on a single day
questions.learningObjective: read a novel's episode structure as an argument about scale
questions.stem: Ulysses, published in 1922, is divided into eighteen episodes and follows a small number of people through one day, and each episode is written in a different prose style, from a broad comic account of ordinary morning to an interior monologue at the end. What does that structure do?

options.text: It fragments the book, since a different style in every episode means a reader has to learn a new book eighteen times
options.misconception: confuses variety of style with disconnection

options.text: It parodies the epic, since a comparison with an ancient poem's twenty-four books is a joke about an old man's journey being too small for one
options.misconception: turns a structural comparison into a parody without evidence that the book is aiming at one

options.text: It postpones the ending, since the final episode is given to an interior voice and therefore arrives after the day's events that a reader has been waiting for
options.misconception: describes a structural choice as a postponement of a plot resolution

options.text: It makes the day's ordinariness the point, since the styles make a reader notice that a life is a sequence of different kinds of attention and that the sequence can be stopped anywhere

questions.explanation: Eighteen episodes and one day is a claim about proportion. A reader who has been given a whole day and a small number of people is being told that the interesting thing is not what a long life does but what a day consists of, and the changing styles are the evidence: the same street can be reported comically in the morning and entered through somebody's interiority at night, and the difference is not a difference of event. Stopping anywhere in the sequence is part of the design, because a book built this way has no privileged point at which the meaning sits. The last episode is the one place where a reader is put inside a consciousness for long enough to be made to choose between the day's outward account and the day's inward one, and the book's refusal to say which is better is the argument. The second option treats variety as disconnection, the third asserts a target the book need not be aiming at, and the fourth reads a deliberate structural choice as a delayed ending.
questions.hint: Ask why the styles change if the day is the only thing that changes.

questions.topic: The Little Review prosecution and what it decided
questions.learningObjective: read a legal outcome at the level of what it actually established
questions.stem: After Ulysses was serialised in an American literary magazine, the magazine's editors were prosecuted in 1921, the numbers that had appeared were destroyed, and the completed book was then published in Paris in 1922 and not admitted to American circulation for years afterwards. What did the case establish?

options.text: That the novel was held obscene, since a prosecution and a destruction of copies is a verdict on the book
options.misconception: reads a conviction of publishers as a verdict on the work

options.text: That the magazine was convicted and the magazine could not print the work, which is a fact about a periodical and not a ruling on the novel's standing
That the novel was permanently banned, since a destroyed printing cannot be replaced by a later one
options.misconception: supposes a destruction of copies is permanent when a Paris edition followed

options.text: That the case established what literature is, since a court that convicts a publisher has decided a question of aesthetics
options.misconception: credits a court with a question of taste that it did not decide

questions.explanation: The distinction the item is about is the one that was actually contested afterwards: the proceeding was against the magazine's publishers, and what was stopped was a serialisation. A reader who says the novel was held obscene has moved one step further than the record goes, and a reader who says a court decided what literature is has moved several steps. What the case did establish is a practical fact with a long tail: an American publisher would not risk the work, an American reader could not buy it, and a Parisian publisher would. That is a history of circulation rather than of a text, and it matters because it means the book's first complete readers were not the readers it was written for. The third option mistakes the destruction of one printing for a permanent ban, and the fourth mistakes a conviction for a ruling on aesthetics. None of this makes the case uninteresting; it makes the case about something other than what it is often said to be about.
questions.hint: Ask who was prosecuted and what was destroyed.

questions.topic: Mrs Dalloway and its two narrative threads
questions.learningObjective: read two interleaved threads as one argument rather than two stories
questions.stem: Mrs Dalloway, published in 1925, follows a woman preparing to give a party across a single day and a shell-shocked man who has come to the city to die, and the book moves between the two, and the last of its sections is a report of a death and its aftermath. What does the book's method do?

options.text: It supplies a second plot, since a novel about a party needs another story to give the party something to interrupt
options.misconception: treats a thread as a plot added for a structural purpose

options.text: It contrasts sanity and madness, since one thread is ordinary and the other is not and the book is therefore a comparison
options.misconception: reduces the method to a contrast, which is the reading the book works hardest to prevent

options.text: It makes one day a measure of another, since a party and a suicide are not the same kind of event and a reader who has followed both has been asked to hold them in one frame
It withholds the connection, since the book never says why the man is there and a reader is left to supply the reason
options.misconception: claims a withheld link that the book supplies at the end

questions.explanation: The method is juxtaposition and the argument is proportion. A party and a suicide are not commensurable, and a book that runs them in the same day is asking a reader to notice that a day can contain both without one explaining the other. That is a harder thing to hold than a parallel plot, because a parallel plot usually arrives with a comparison attached; here the comparison has to be made by the reader, and it changes as the day goes on, because the party gets brighter while the other thread gets darker and the two are close enough to look like one thing seen from two ends. The final section, which is a report rather than a scene, is what makes the method possible, since it settles the question the book has been asking without explaining it. The second option reduces the second thread to a device, the third turns the method into a comparison between sanity and madness, and the fourth claims a withheld link that the book supplies.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has to do to hold two non-comparable kinds of event in one frame.

questions.topic: The Sound and the Fury and the dates of its four sections
questions.learningObjective: read a book's section order as a sequence of perspectives
questions.stem: Four sections of The Sound and the Fury, published in 1929, have been printed out of order. Restore them so that each is placed after the one whose time it continues or the one whose limits it exposes.

options.text: a section given to a young boy on a single afternoon, in which the reader is held inside a mind that cannot hold time and cannot tell events in order
a section in a college town in a single week, in a young man who has just learned something about his father and is going to do something unforgivable
a section given to a man of middle age running a business, in which the events are clear, datable and monotonous and the reader can see exactly how little time is passing
a section given to a narrator on a day that has already happened, in which the book reports itself and its readers and admits what it has cost

questions.explanation: The four sections are four different relations to time and the order is the argument. The first is a child's, where time does not pass so much as arrive, and everything that happens happens at once; nothing can be later than anything else. The second moves back to a college town and a young man, and the time is now narrow and dated, which is the point, because this is a mind that has organised its world into a single decisive afternoon and cannot stop. The third is the section that looks like a business day, and its clarity is the joke and the cruelty: for a man who has made his life a matter of arithmetic, time has become a flat surface on which nothing registers. The fourth is the only one in which a narrator can talk about the other three, and it comes last because it can only speak from outside them. The order cannot begin with the second, because it presupposes a family and a history; it cannot begin with the third or the fourth, because both need what the first two supply.
questions.hint: Ask which section needs the family and the history the others presuppose.

questions.topic: Animal Farm's first American edition and the subtitle it dropped
questions.learningObjective: read a dropped subtitle as a decision about a book's readers
questions.stem: Animal Farm was published in Britain in 1945 with the subtitle A Fairy Story, and the American edition of 1946 was issued without it, and the American edition also printed a tenth chapter that later printings left out. What do those two differences add up to?

options.text: That the book is two books, since a text that changes between editions cannot be a single work
options.misconception: collapses an edition into a work, which is the reverse of the truth

options.text: That the British edition is the true one, since the author's own country and the author's own subtitle outrank a foreign printing
options.misconception: argues priority from nationality, which the evidence does not supply

options.text: That the tenth chapter was a printing error, since a chapter that had to be withdrawn can hardly have been part of the work
options.misconception: assumes a withdrawn chapter was an accident

options.text: That the two editions are two interventions in the book, and a reader who has seen only one of them has met an authorial decision rather than a neutral text

questions.explanation: A dropped subtitle and a withdrawn chapter are both decisions, and decisions are evidence. Dropping the subtitle says to a reader that the book is not to be taken as a children's story, which is a claim about tone made by somebody other than the author; withdrawing the tenth chapter says that a section is not to be read, and the fact that copies with it exist makes the decision permanent and inspectable. Neither decision is invisible and neither is neutral, so a reader who wants to know what the book is has to know which edition is in hand. The important methodological point is that this is normal. Books are changed on the way to the public and readers inherit the changes as though they were the original. The second option confuses an edition with a work, the third argues priority from a writer's nationality, and the fourth mistakes a decision for an error, which is the reading that makes the whole enterprise of textual history invisible.
questions.hint: Ask who took each decision, and what a reader is left holding.

questions.topic: Animal Farm's names and the form they make
questions.learningObjective: read an allegorical naming as a claim about what stands for what
questions.stem: In Animal Farm the animals are given the names of a political class, two of the leaders are given the names of a revolution's opposing figures, and the farmhouse is run under a system that its keepers describe in a vocabulary of command. What does the naming do that a plain allegorical label would not?

options.text: It prevents the reader from applying the book to anything, since a name taken from history is a substitution and a substitution cannot be read as a real case
options.misconception: supposes that a substitution cannot be read as a case, which is the whole point of one

options.text: It supplies a reader with prior knowledge, so that a name brings a history into a barnyard and the reader's familiarity becomes part of the joke and part of the argument
It makes the book a key, since a reader who recognises every name can decode every event and the decoding is the reading
options.misconception: reduces the book to a code and mistakes the availability of a key for the whole of the work

options.text: It removes the animals' individuality, since a name taken from a politician makes a pig a politician and a reader can forget the pig
options.misconception: supposes that a name displaces a character, which is the opposite of what a name does

questions.explanation: Allegory is often taught as a code to be decoded, and a book built on names invites exactly that reading. The better account is that the names bring a history with them. The book's own vocabulary then does the rest: the system the animals build is described in the words of administration, and a reader can hear the words changing meaning as the animals use them. The second option says a substitution cannot be read as a case, which would empty the form. The third reduces the book to a code and forgets that the reader's knowledge is a resource rather than a solution. The fourth imagines that a name displaces a character rather than sharpening one.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader brings to the book that the book does not have to state.

questions.topic: Nineteen Eighty-Four and its appendix on the new language
questions.learningObjective: read an appendix as an argument about a language rather than about a plot
questions.stem: Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949, ends with an appendix presented as an essay on the principles of a new language, written by a scholar and not by the author, and it explains that the language is designed so that most of what people might want to say cannot be said. What does that appendix do?

options.text: It settles the book, since an appendix that explains the mechanism tells a reader exactly how the thing works and nothing more is needed
options.misconception: mistakes an explanation for a resolution

options.text: It weakens the book, since a fiction that publishes its own instructions has given away the trick and can no longer surprise
options.misconception: assumes that an explained mechanism cannot still be effective in a narrative

options.text: It turns the whole book into an argument about language, since a reader who has read a chapter about a language being designed to prevent thought cannot afterwards read the chapters about what people are made to say as mere plot
It dates the book, since a language project of this kind belongs to a particular decade's anxieties
options.misconception: infers a date from a theme, which is the opposite of dating

questions.explanation: The appendix is the most efficient thing in the book, and it is efficient because of what it is written as. It is a technical essay, competently argued, with a scholarly apparatus, and it explains a design principle rather than a plot: that a vocabulary can be constructed so that certain thoughts have no form to take. Once a reader has that in hand, the earlier chapters stop being incidents. The language of the party, the slogans, the instructions about thought, the invented words that are difficult to say aloud, the apparent contradictions that a reader can only resolve by a kind of translation: all of them are now the same project seen at different distances. A reader who has the appendix will notice the difficulty of certain sentences as a designed difficulty rather than a stylistic one. The second option confuses an explanation with a resolution, the third believes an explained mechanism cannot be effective in a story, and the fourth dates the book from a theme, which tells a reader nothing at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader does differently after reading the last eleven pages.

questions.topic: Two serial novels serialised for two different reasons
questions.learningObjective: compare two books printed in instalments for different audiences and purposes
questions.stem: Uncle Tom's Cabin was printed in instalments in a Washington weekly that was already arguing a case, and Our Mutual Friend began in a London periodical and was issued at intervals dictated by production. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The two are the same arrangement, since a novel printed in parts is always printed in parts for the same reason
options.misconception: supplies one motive for all serialisation, which the two cases do not share

options.text: The first was a novel and the second was a pamphlet, since a story that appears in a newspaper has left the form of the novel behind it
options.misconception: changes the form of a work by changing its venue

options.text: The second was the better received, since a book that must find its readership is the one a reader will hear more about
options.misconception: infers reception from a production schedule, which is not what a schedule records

options.text: The two were written into different situations, so the first had an audience that had already agreed and the second had to recruit one, and the instalments bear that difference

questions.explanation: The comparison worth making is between the audience each serial had, because that is what the instalments had to do. A paper already arguing a case gives a writer a readership that has arrived with its own vocabulary, and the instalment can be written as one more piece of an argument in progress, which is why a serial in such a paper can be interrupted and resumed without losing its thread. A commercial periodical is under a different constraint: it has to hold a reader who has not yet decided to care, and it has to do so at intervals it does not choose, which is why a gap in the middle of such a serial is a different event from a regular instalment. The second option gives one motive for all serialisation, the third changes a work's form by changing its venue, and the fourth infers reception from a production schedule, which is not a thing a schedule records.
questions.hint: Ask what the first instalment had to achieve in each case.

questions.topic: A serial novel's parts and the order a reader meets them
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the order of composition from the order of reading

options.text: the finished manuscript, which is the state of the text before anybody else has touched it
the first monthly part, which is the first public existence of the story and the first point at which a reader can begin to judge it
the last monthly part, which closes the sequence in the only order a subscriber ever experienced
the publisher's proof of the first part, which is the first state in which a compositor or an editor can have altered the text
a later reprint that reprints the whole text at once, so that a reader for the first time meets the book in a single volume

questions.explanation: Three sequences are at work and the order follows from keeping them apart. The manuscript comes first because everything downstream depends on it. The proof of the first part comes next, because it is the earliest moment at which anybody other than the author can have changed a word, and a reader who wants to know about a serial's text has to begin there. The first monthly part follows the proof, since it is the first public state; the last part follows the first, since a serial is read in order and a reader who begins at the end is a reader of a different book. The reprint comes last, and it is a distinct event rather than a restoration, because a reader meeting the whole text at once meets a sequence that no subscriber ever met. The order cannot be rearranged, because each step's authority depends on the ones before it, and the last step is not a return to the beginning but a new way of meeting the same text.

What does the fifth part do that a fourth part could not?

options.text: It adds a plot, since an event's aftermath is a new set of events and a book that ends inside the event has been cut short
options.misconception: treats an afterword as an additional plot

options.text: It weakens the book, since a book that survives its own subject has lost the intensity that made it worth reading
options.misconception: judges an afterword as a loss of intensity, which is a criticism of a choice rather than of its effect

options.text: It apologises for the book, since a writer who returns after the event has doubts about what was written during it
options.misconception: reads a change of scale as a retraction

options.text: It changes the tense of the book's claim, since a narrative inside an event can only be testimony, and a section after the event can judge the event and be judged against what followed

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What serial publication obliges an author to do
questions.learningObjective: state the constraints a publication form places on composition
questions.stem: A novelist is writing a book to be issued in monthly parts, and a reader is following it as it appears. Explain what the arrangement obliges the author to do that a book printed all at once would not, and what it forbids.

answer.exemplar: Serial publication changes composition in three places. First, at the end of each part, the writer must supply a small completion: a question answered, a stage reached, a piece of information landed, so that a reader who buys the next part has been repaid. Where a novel can only end properly once, the middle of a serial becomes the difficult part, and a writer will use more than one device to get through it, such as a turn inside a part or a narrator who comments at the end of one. Second, the format forbids hoarding. A book whose method is withheld information will spend its supply before the final part, and a long digression is dangerous because a single part cannot be filled with one. Third, it makes revision expensive, because four months of readers have a claim on the characters they have been following, and a change made late will be read as a betrayal rather than a discovery. A fourth point is not about form at all and a full answer will include it: the arrangement is commercial, and a reader who has paid and waited is an audience with expectations that a volume does not have. The best evidence for any of this is a set of closings: read the last page of each of the first few parts and the techniques become visible. The mistake is to treat serialisation as a mere inconvenience, since almost every convention such a book is remembered by was invented to solve one of these problems.

questions.explanation: The useful way to answer is to work part by part and then to say what the format forbids. Every instalment must end with enough of a thing completed to satisfy a reader who buys the next part, and that means each part needs a small shape of its own: a question answered, a stage of a journey reached, a piece of information landed. A novel that can only end properly once will be in trouble, and the difficulty is greatest in the middle, where an instalment must interrupt without seeming arbitrary. Several devices solve this and a writer will use more than one: a turn inside a part, a narrator who comments at the end of one, a chapter that closes on a question, a shape that recurs and can be interrupted. What the format forbids is as important. It forbids holding everything back: a novel whose whole method is withheld information will exhaust its supply before the last part. It also makes a long digression dangerous, because a part cannot be filled with one; and it makes retconception expensive, since a reader who has read four months of a book has a claim on the people in it that a later volume may not be able to satisfy. The best answers will add the commercial and the personal, because the arrangement is not only a formal one: a reader who has paid and waited is an audience with expectations, and the person writing for that audience is not writing the same book as the person writing a volume. The mistake to avoid is describing the format as a mere inconvenience, since almost every convention the book is remembered by is a solution to one of these problems.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true at the end of every part, and what must be withheld until the last one.

questions.topic: What a reader should do with a disputed ending
questions.learningObjective: set out a method for reading an ending that critics disagree about
questions.stem: A famous novel has an ending that some readers find satisfying, some find evasive, and some find both, and the writer said one thing about it at one moment and something else at another. Explain how a reader should proceed who wants a defensible account of the ending rather than a preference for one of them.

answer.exemplar: The method has three steps and the order matters. First, describe the ending without interpreting it: who acts, what is said, what is withheld, and what the reader is required to do next. Many disagreements about endings turn out to be disagreements about events in the last chapter, and settling the description settles them. Second, sort the evidence into kinds. The text is one kind and cannot be argued with; the writer's statements are another, and since they conflict, both should be kept as claims rather than one being chosen quietly. Third, ask what each kind of evidence can establish. A writer's remark establishes an intention at a moment; it cannot establish what a text does. So where the two disagree, the text settles the description of the book, and the disagreement itself becomes part of the ending's history, often the most interesting part. From this a reader can say three things: what the ending claims, what the writer wanted it to claim, and whether the gap is a failure or the design. A complete answer will add what would change the account, usually a dated document or an earlier draft, and what cannot change it, which is a reader's preference. The failure to avoid is choosing a reading because it is liked, which yields a verdict but not an account.

questions.explanation: A defensible account can be built in three moves, and the order matters. First, describe the ending precisely, without interpreting it: who acts, what is said, what is left unsaid, and what a reader is asked to do next. Too many disputes about endings are really disputes about what happens in the last chapter, and precision removes them. Second, sort the evidence by kind. The text is one kind of evidence and it cannot be argued with; the writer's statements are another kind, and they are inconsistent, so the honest move is to treat the earlier and the later as two claims rather than choosing silently. Third, decide what each kind of evidence can do. A writer's statement can tell a reader what a writer intended at a moment; it cannot tell a reader what a text does, and where the two conflict the text wins for the purposes of describing the book, while the conflict itself becomes evidence about the ending's history. From there a reader can say what the ending claims, what the writer wanted it to claim, and whether the gap between them is a flaw or the point. The mistake to avoid is settling the question by liking one reading better, because that produces no account a reader could show to somebody who disliked it.
questions.hint: Ask what can be established from the text, what from the writer's statements, and what the difference between them is worth.

questions.topic: The 1623 Folio and the plays that appeared in it for the first time
questions.learningObjective: read a first edition's contents as a claim about a body's work
questions.stem: The Folio of 1623 gathered thirty-six plays and printed eighteen of them for the first time, and it did so in folio rather than in the quarto format in which plays had usually been published, and it carried commendatory verses and an address to the reader. What does that collection amount to?

options.text: A body of work being gathered by others than its author, since a volume assembled after a writer's death is a claim about the shape of that work made by people with their own reasons
A publishers error, since a writer who did not arrange the volume cannot have intended the contents and the order must therefore be accidental
options.misconception: supplies an intention the author could not have had and calls it a criticism

options.text: A complete canon, since a collected edition fixes what belongs and anything left out is thereby excluded for good
options.misconception: treats a first collection as a closed canon, which it cannot be

options.text: A critical edition, since a volume with prefatory matter is presenting texts and therefore must be establishing them
options.misconception: confuses prefatory matter with textual editing

questions.explanation: The Folio is a document about how a body of work came to exist, and it should be read as one, because nothing in the volume was arranged by the writer whose plays it prints. That is the interesting part and it is also why the volume is evidence rather than a convenience. Eighteen plays appearing for the first time in a collected edition means eighteen plays whose earlier existence was in the main theatrical rather than printed, and their presence in a book changes what can be said about them: they can now be read, compared, and set against one another. The format follows from the scale, since thirty-six long plays will not go into thirty-six thin quarto volumes, and the prefatory matter does the ordinary work of a book that wants to be taken seriously. What a first collection cannot do is fix a canon, because it is the first and others will follow. The second, third and fourth options each mistake the volume's status for something it does not claim.
questions.hint: Ask who decided what the volume contains, and what that means for the question of canonicity.
